items.title: Hybrid AI Agentic Framework and Machine Vision for Automated Preliminary Root Cause Analysis in Wind Turbine Alarm Systems Using Multi Modal Data Fusion
items.abstract: Wind turbine systems are frequently subjected to complex operational conditions, leading to frequent quality issues that trigger warnings and alarms, and this demands rapid and accurate quality check with Root Cause Analysis (RCA). Conventional RCA processes rely fully on manual inspection and expert interpretation that involves human, resulting in significant time delays, increased operational costs, and high turbine downtime. To address these challenges, this paper presents a Hybrid AI Agent Framework that integrates Machine Vision and Multi Modal Data Fusion for automated preliminary RCA in wind turbine alarm systems. The proposed system consists of YOLO based machine vision for physical defect detection, advanced thermal image analysis for temperature anomaly identification, and historical SCADA data integration to generate a comprehensive diagnostic context. A novel AI agent-based RCA engine is developed, which synthesizes multi source inputs and produces structured root cause insights using a DMAIC (Define-Measure-Analyse-Improve-Control) framework and that also includes Fishbone and 5-Why quality analytical methodologies from six sigma quality principle. The architecture is implemented using a scalable Fast API based backend, integrated with a user-friendly web interface that has turbine data retrieval, and real time analysis. The system supports both single instance and batch processing, enabling efficient handling of large datasets. Automated alerting mechanisms are incorporated through email notifications, ensuring timely communication of detected anomalies and quality issues. Validation of the system is carried out using synthetic and open-source datasets, demonstrating its capability to accurately identify defects, detect thermal hotspots, and generate meaningful preliminary RCA reports. The proposed framework significantly reduces dependency on manual inspection, minimizes turbine downtime, reduces loss production factor (LPF) and enhances operational efficiency. Overall, the system establishes a scalable and intelligent foundation for future development of fully autonomous wind turbine diagnostics and predictive maintenance solutions.

items.title: Imaging biomarkers of intracranial meningioma consistency: a scoping review of conventional MRI, advanced MRI, radiomics and artificial intelligence techniques
items.abstract: Preoperative prediction of intracranial meningioma consistency may improve surgical planning by anticipating the ease of internal debulking, operative difficulty, and the feasibility of minimally invasive approaches. Numerous imaging biomarkers have been proposed, ranging from routine MRI measurements to advanced quantitative techniques and artificial intelligence-based models. This scoping review aimed to critically evaluate their diagnostic performance, methodological quality, biological rationale, and potential for clinical implementation. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched from database inception to July 2026 in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Original human studies assessing MRI-derived biomarkers for the preoperative prediction of meningioma consistency were eligible. Studies were grouped into routine MRI, advanced MRI, and artificial intelligence-based approaches. Methodological quality was assessed using QUADAS-2, the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale, and the Radiomics Quality Score, as appropriate. Owing to substantial methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively. Thirty-five publications were included: 14 evaluated routine MRI biomarkers, 13 advanced MRI techniques, and 8 radiomics or artificial intelligence approaches. Among routine sequences, T2-weighted signal intensity ratios, particularly the tumor-to-cerebellar peduncle T2-weighted intensity ratio, showed the most consistent association with softer tumors and was the most readily deployable in routine practice. Diffusion-derived parameters provided complementary but less reproducible information. Magnetic resonance elastography demonstrated the strongest evidence among advanced techniques by directly quantifying tissue stiffness and correlating with intraoperative consistency and histopathological features. Radiomics and deep-learning models reported high apparent predictive performance, frequently with AUCs above 0.90, but most studies were retrospective, single-center, internally validated, and in some cases based on overlapping patient cohorts. Routine T2-based biomarkers currently offer the best balance between accessibility and predictive value. Magnetic resonance elastography provides greater biomechanical specificity, whereas artificial intelligence approaches remain promising but insufficiently validated for routine use. Standardized reference standards, multicenter external validation, and stronger biological correlation are required before widespread clinical implementation.

items.title: Immersive VR for Signed Language Learning: A Comparative Evaluation of ASL Vocabulary Production
items.abstract: Limited access to qualified instructors and opportunities for guided practice remains a barrier for many people learning American Sign Language (ASL), including hearing learners and newly signing Deaf people. Interactive technologies that provide real-time, accessible feedback may help lower these barriers and support wider adoption of ASL. We developed ASL Champ!, a standalone virtual reality (VR) application that supports introductory ASL vocabulary learning in immersive environments. ASL Champ! provides automated feedback via a deep learning–based sign recognition algorithm using the VR headset's built-in cameras. We evaluated ASL Champ! in a within-participant experimental study comparing it with a conventional 2D video-based learning platform (Edpuzzle), focusing on user experience, cognitive workload, and behavioral outcomes relevant to accessible learning systems. Adult non-signers ( n = 11) completed matched ASL lessons using ASL Champ! (VR) and Edpuzzle (2D) and completed assessments of receptive ASL comprehension and expressive sign production. Results showed that VR-based learning imposed a higher cognitive workload than the 2D platform, while receptive comprehension was near ceiling across conditions. In contrast, signs learned in VR were produced more accurately, particularly with respect to handshape. Despite the higher workload, most participants preferred the VR platform for continued learning. These findings characterize key design trade-offs in accessible sign language learning technologies and inform the development of future immersive systems for ASL learning.

items.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence algorithms on architectural visualization. A Practical review
items.abstract: This article investigates the creative potential and practical use of artificial intelligence in architectural visualization by testing three free platforms: Fabrie, Mnml AI and LookX AI Cloud, on a real project involving the design of a single-story house with a summer kitchen. The study aims to assess the extent to which these AI tools can support or enhance the development and refinement of architectural visualizations, both through the generation of new renders based on conceptual sketches and through the processing of existing visual data. The methodology involves the comparative analysis of the platforms’ outputs using four evaluation criteria: clarity of spatial perception, level of detailing, emotional expressiveness, and the format and quality of the final exported visual data. Based on this framework, the study identifies the respective strengths and limitations of each AI system, highlighting distinctive characteristics in render quality, user interface, and interpretive responsiveness to design prompts. The article also formulates practical guidelines for data preparation and prompt formulation, addressing technical constraints, model sensitivity, and the iterative nature of human-AI interaction. A key contribution of the study lies in its dual methodological approach: rendering experiments were conducted in two modes: generation from a blank sketch and enhancement of an existing render, thereby illuminating how AI tools can be integrated into different phases of the design workflow. The study also reflects on the broader implications of human-AI collaboration in architectural practice, focusing on how authorship, visual language, and creative decision-making are redefined in the context of automated design assistance. The scientific novelty of this research lies in its detailed, real-case-based evaluation of emerging AI visualization platforms in architectural work. Its practical significance is evident in the set of recommendations it provides to architects, designers, and educators exploring AI as a co-creative design partner.

items.title: Impact of Explainable Artificial Intelligence on User Trust, Privacy Perception, and Content Engagement in Social Media Platforms
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is widely used by social media platforms to personalize feeds, recommend videos, suggest accounts, and select advertisements.However, users may not understand why a particular item appears or how their data influences these recommendations.Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) aims to make AI outputs more understandable to people.This paper presents a survey-based research framework for examining the relationship between perceived explanation clarity and usefulness, user trust, privacy perception, and willingness to engage with recommended content.A questionnaire with demographic questions and five-point response scales is proposed.To demonstrate the planned analysis, a simulated dataset of 150 records is used for descriptive illustration.In this simulated dataset, mean ratings were 3.43 for explanation clarity, 3.54 for explanation usefulness, 3.19 for trust, 3.50 for privacy confidence, and 3.30 for engagement willingness on a five-point scale.These figures are illustrative only and do not represent real participants or establish real-world relationships.The paper outlines a methodology for collecting genuine responses and analysing them using descriptive statistics, reliability checks, correlation, and regression where appropriate.The work highlights the need to consider both transparency and privacy when designing user-centred AI recommendations.

items.title: Impact of Robotics and Automation in Material Recovery
items.abstract: Automation and robots are redefining the material recovery system by bringing precision, efficiency, and scalability to processes of waste management and recycling. Conventional forms of waste recovery have been associated with a number of causative factors that have limited their effectiveness, including labor-intensive activities, safety issues, and ineffective sorting and processing mechanisms of various waste streams. The combination of advanced robotics, artificial intelligence, machine vision, and machine learning makes the automated systems have a higher level of accuracy and pace at which they separate and process recyclable materials. Co-robots (cobots) are also added to these processes to be safer and more flexible, working in parallel with people, minimizing work hazards and increasing productivity. The following chapter discusses the contribution of robotics and automation in material recovery, with particular emphasis on the use of these technologies to sort waste, dismantle it, and extract resources. It also includes case studies showing how effective they have been in the process of achieving a circular economy, challenges encountered; including implementation cost, energy use, and barriers to technological adaptation. In essence, material recovery solutions powered by robotics play a part in a sustainable process of resource valorization and help in fast-tracking the shift to a zero-waste, circular economy.

items.title: Implementing a Futures-Instructional Design
items.abstract: Chapter 11 examines how schools can redesign instructional delivery systems to prepare students for an increasingly complex, technology-driven future. The chapter introduces the concept of an instructional contract that shifts the focus from standardized performance measures to personalized, futures-oriented learning experiences for students. It explores emerging pedagogical approaches including student-centered, culturally responsive, and technology-enhanced learning, and highlights the growing influence of artificial intelligence and data-informed instruction. The chapter also examines synchronous, asynchronous, in-person, and virtual learning models, emphasizing the need for flexible instructional designs tailored to individual learner profiles. Central to this work is coherence, ensuring alignment of curriculum, assessment, and instruction with futures-ready competencies such as creativity, analytical thinking, resilience, technological literacy, and life-long learning. The chapter concludes by demonstrating how instructional design is the connecting framework that brings assessment and curriculum together in a futures-literate system, creating coherence across learner profiles, instructional practices, and futures-ready competencies to support student success in an ever-changing world.

items.title: Implementing Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Decision Support, Diagnostics And Predictive Analytics In Healthcare: A domain-contingent AI implementation model
items.abstract: Objective: The study aimed to analyse Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques for clinical decision support, diagnostic analysis and predictive analytics for better implementation in healthcare. Design: The study adopted a systematic literature review guided by Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines to identify 17 studies related to three domains: clinical decision support, diagnostic analysis and predictive analytics. Thematic analysis was conducted to propose a conceptual model, the Domain-Contingent AI Implementation Model in Healthcare, to suggest that AI effectiveness relies on the domain-specific drivers, constraints, and system-level enablers. Main outcome measures: The study evaluates AI implementation against the drivers and constraints of three domains, derived through thematic analysis in healthcare settings. Results: Findings emphasised the nature of AI as a domain-contingent capability across the three healthcare domains. AI effectiveness in healthcare is driven by interpretability, data intensity and forecasting power, while it is constrained by trust, black-box models and a validation gap in clinical decision support, diagnostic analysis and predictive analytics, respectively. Conclusion: The study concluded that AI’s effectiveness in healthcare implementation is driven by adaptation factors, including usability, infrastructure, and reliability.

items.title: Improving AI Explainability Through Design of Experiments
items.abstract: ABSTRACT In artificial intelligence (AI), the complexity of many models and processes surpasses human understanding, making it challenging to determine why a specific prediction is made. This lack of transparency is particularly problematic in critical fields like healthcare, where trust in a model's predictions is paramount. As a result, the explainability of machine learning (ML) models, as well as other complex models, has become a key area of focus. Efforts to improve model explainability often involve experimenting with AI systems and approximating their behavior through interpretable surrogate mechanisms. However, these procedures can be resource‐intensive. Optimal experimental design (OED), which seeks to maximize the information obtained from a limited number of observations, offers promising methods for improving the efficiency of these explainability techniques. To demonstrate this potential, we explore Local Interpretable Model‐agnostic Explanations (LIME), a widely used method introduced in 2016. LIME provides explanations by generating new data points near the instance of interest and passing them through the model. While effective, this process can be computationally expensive, especially when predictions are costly or require many samples. LIME is highly versatile and can be applied to a wide range of models and datasets. In this work, we focus on models involving tabular data, regression tasks, and linear models as interpretable local approximations. By utilizing optimal design of experiments' techniques, we reduce the number of function evaluations of the complex model, thereby reducing the computational effort of LIME by a substantial amount. We consider this modified version of LIME to be energy‐efficient, and thus preferable.

items.title: Improving dysarthric speech classification with generative AI-based data augmentation
items.abstract: Dysarthria is a neurological speech disorder characterized by impaired motor control of speech production, resulting in reduced intelligibility. It commonly arises in the context of neurodegenerative conditions, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and cerebral palsy. The development of deep learning systems for dysarthria assessment is hindered by the scarcity of annotated data, which restricts the ability of models to generalize to unseen speakers. This study proposes a cross-corpus diffusion-based data augmentation strategy for improving automatic speech intelligibility classification from dysarthric speech. A Grad-TTS model is trained on dysarthric speakers from the TORGO dataset and used to synthesize the vocabulary of UA-Speech, producing speaker-conditioned samples intended to transfer pathological acoustic traits across corpora. The proposed strategy is evaluated both independently and in combination with conventional signal-level augmentation using ResNet-50 and ResNet-152 classifiers in binary and four-class intelligibility classification tasks. The results indicate that cross-corpus synthetic augmentation improves average performance and that, in most settings, its integration with conventional augmentation yields further gains, suggesting that the two strategies introduce complementary forms of variability.

items.title: Instrument-mediated activity: Towards a milieu-centred approach beyond techno-solutionism
items.abstract: BackgroundDigital technologies are promoted to support sustainability transitions, yet their contribution depends on how they are appropriated in activity rather than on technical performance alone.ObjectiveThis article examines the role of technologies in socio-ecological transitions through an activity-centred ergonomics perspective. Drawing on the instrumental approach, it analyses how digital and precision technologies become-or fail to become-instruments for activity in two sectors targeted by sustainability policies: domestic energy management and agriculture.MethodsThe study combines a longitudinal analysis of smart-grid interfaces (SOLENN project) and a cross-case synthesis of four precision agriculture technology (PAT) studies. Although the contexts differ, both are analysed using the same framework grounded in activity-centred ergonomics and the instrumental approach, focusing on epistemic, pragmatic, reflexive, and interpersonal mediations. This framework enables the identification of mechanisms of technology appropriation across sustainability contexts.ResultsTechnological effects do not depend on technical performance alone, but on appropriation processes and instrumental mediations. In domestic energy management, a minority of households stabilised smart-grid interface use when knowledge, motivation, and monitoring practices were present. In agriculture, technologies can support precision, comfort, and temporal flexibility, but also generate reliability work, cognitive load, and transformations in relations with living systems. Across both contexts, findings reveal mechanisms linking use to activity and appropriation.ConclusionsThe findings challenge techno-solutionist approaches by showing that sustainable transitions depend less on technological deployment than on conditions enabling activity. They support a milieu-centred design approach integrating activity, health, collective regulation, and relationships with living environments as sustainability criteria.

items.abstract: This article presents a systematic literature review on the use of emerging technologies in education, with the aim of analyzing their integration into teaching practice and their contribution to improving teaching and learning processes. The literature search was conducted in high-impact, indexed scientific databases, such as Scopus, Web of Science (WoS), Lantidex, SciELO, and Redalyc, covering publications from 2020 to 2025. A total of 836 published scientific articles were retrieved, from which, through a rigorous screening process and application of inclusion and exclusion criteria, 90 articles, both theoretical and empirical, relevant to the review's objectives were selected. The results show a sustained increase in scientific production, particularly since 2020, with a strong emphasis on the use of artificial intelligence, digital platforms, and virtual learning environments. However, the studies analyzed agree that the effectiveness of these technologies depends largely on teachers' pedagogical and digital skills, as well as the existence of clear pedagogical models and ongoing teacher training. Challenges related to the digital divide, resistance to change, and ethical considerations linked to the responsible use of emerging technologies are also identified. It is concluded that their effective integration requires a critical, ethical, and inclusive pedagogical approach aimed at improving the quality of education.

items.title: Integrating Large Language Models and Agent-Based Simulation for Construction Safety Behavior Management: Strategy Focusing and Explainable Report Generation
items.abstract: Unsafe behaviors by construction personnel are the primary cause of construction accidents. How to rationally allocate management resources within limited constraints is a core challenge in construction safety management. This study develops and validates a workflow framework integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) and Agent-Based Modeling (ABM), termed LLM-ABM, aimed at achieving intelligent focusing of management strategies and automated interpretation of simulation results. First, an ABM model was constructed in the context of petroleum engineering to analyze the association between different management resource allocations and the evolutionary outcomes of unsafe behaviors under this specific engineering scenario. Second, a complete response surface comprising 231 combinations with a step size of 0.05 was constructed as an evaluation benchmark. On this basis, a manually designed search framework-guided two-round iterative search flow of the LLM-ABM was developed, and ten rounds of independent comparative experiments were conducted against random search to evaluate its strategy-focusing capability. Subsequently, the simulation results were fed into the LLM, and three experts were invited to evaluate the quality of the generated reports from the perspectives of data fidelity, logical coherence, and recommendation actionability. The comparison of the four typical strategies showed that, under the current model settings, active management was associated with a lower mean unsafe personnel ratio (J = 8.05%) and a lower peak unsafe personnel ratio (Pmax = 10.43%), while the balanced strategy was associated with maintaining late-stage average safe personnel ratio (Slate = 60.63%). In terms of strategy focusing, under the current discrete grid with a step size of 0.05 and fixed ABM model settings, the Top-10% hit rate of LLM-ABM reached 20.00%, numerically higher than the 9.50% of random search. Moreover, the final selected strategies exhibit better global rankings on the discrete grid with lower variance. Although this difference did not reach statistical significance due to the limited number of trials, the large effect size preliminarily suggests that LLM-ABM has the potential to focus search resources on high-quality strategy regions. Regarding report generation, expert evaluations yielded scores of 0.95 for data fidelity, 0.87 for logical coherence, and 0.85 for recommendation actionability. This study preliminarily demonstrates that the LLM-ABM workflow possesses the potential to focus search on high-quality strategy regions under a limited budget, as well as the feasibility of transforming structured simulation data into traceable management recommendations, providing a complete technical pathway of “generation–evaluation–feedback–interpretation” for construction safety management in petroleum engineering.

items.title: Integrating large language models and expert knowledge to identify risk factors and predict mode of delivery with machine learning
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Accurately predicting the mode of delivery is a significant challenge in obstetrics, with implications for maternal healthcare planning, resource allocation, and personalized patient counseling. While machine learning offers promising predictive capabilities, the selection of relevant clinical and socioeconomic risk factors from vast possibilities remains a critical and nontrivial step that directly affects model performance and clinical utility. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to (1) predict the mode of delivery (vaginal vs. cesarean) using machine learning algorithms and (2) identify the key risk factors influencing delivery mode prediction. METHODS: A retrospective study was conducted on eligible pregnant women who delivered at Bent-Al-Huda Hospital in Bojnourd, Iran. A hybrid feature identification approach was employed: large language models (LLMs) initially proposed 63 potential risk factors. Through iterative refinement involving domain experts and assessment of data availability and frequency, this list was consolidated to 35 final variables for modeling. Machine learning algorithms, including multilayer perceptron (MLP), decision tree, naïve Bayes, and support vector machine (SVM), were applied to build predictive models. RESULTS: Among all models, SVM showed the best performance using all features, achieving an accuracy of 94.8% and an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.94. Decision tree analysis identified previous cesarean section history, insurance type, and fetal presentation as the three most important predictive factors. After excluding 40 women with prior cesarean delivery, SVM maintained robust performance with accuracy of 94.3% and an AUC of 0.92. Using antenatal features only, MLP achieved the highest accuracy before and after excluding women with previous cesarean section (92.9% and 92.2%), while SVM also showed the highest discriminative ability (accuracy 92.4%, AUC 0.90 and accuracy 91.3%, AUC 0.87, respectively). CONCLUSION: This study demonstrates that combining expert knowledge with LLMs enables effective risk factor identification and that careful feature selection allows the proposed model to predict delivery type with high accuracy.

items.title: Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Enhancing Teaching Practices
items.abstract: Large Language models have revolutionised educational approaches across the knowledge spectrum, infusing innovative teaching methods that prioritise student engagement in classroom activities. This article focuses on LLM models in education-centric settings with a teacher focus, aiming to facilitate academic activities. The framework focuses on the key features of the following AI tool platforms: Khanmigo, Diffit, Brisk Teach AI, and eduaide. The study integrated an autoethnographic approach, applied the active learning theory, and Technological Pedagogical Knowledge (TPK) as the theoretical framework, aligned with the study's context. Key teaching functional features of these tools are assessed under the theme: accessibility, open and paid features, user interface, language adaptability, forms of generated content, and assessment. The analysis revealed that these LLM platforms had practical functional features for rationalising teachers' academic activities. It also highlights the importance of educators' roles in integrating AI-generated material thoughtfully for effective teaching and learning.

items.title: Inteligencia artificial en la educación superior: revisión sistemática
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is progressively transforming higher education by incorporating tools capable of supporting teaching, learning, personalization, and feedback. However, its adoption poses challenges related to teacher competencies, technological infrastructure, and the need to establish ethical guidelines for its use. Objective: To analyze the use of artificial intelligence in higher education based on recent scientific evidence. Methodology: A systematic review was conducted following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. The search was performed in the Scopus, Web of Science, and SciELO databases using search terms in Spanish and English. After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, 34 articles published between 2024 and 2025 were selected for analysis. Results: The reviewed studies showed that AI-based tools, particularly ChatGPT, can promote pedagogical innovation, personalized learning, and academic feedback. Opportunities were also identified to optimize specific educational activities and expand possibilities for student support. However, limitations persist regarding insufficient teacher training, digital infrastructure and connectivity gaps, and the absence of robust institutional mechanisms for ethical governance. Conclusions: AI has the potential to strengthen teaching and learning processes in higher education, provided that its integration is accompanied by inclusive institutional policies, continuous teacher training, and guidelines promoting the critical, responsible, and ethical use of these technologies.

items.title: Inteligencia artificial generativa en la Educación Media Superior: aplicaciones, resultados, desafíos y consideraciones éticas. Una revisión sistemática
items.abstract: This systematic review examined the applications, outcomes, challenges, and ethical considerations of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in upper secondary education. Studies published between 2022 and August 2026 were searched in Google Scholar, SciELO, Redalyc, and Dialnet. The final corpus comprised 32 unique empirical studies, examined through an integrative qualitative synthesis. Applications included writing, language learning, mathematics, science, programming, tutoring, and feedback. Findings were heterogeneous, including positive, null, negative, and mixed outcomes. Perceived usefulness and AI-assisted performance do not necessarily indicate independent learning. Key challenges involved cognitive dependence, reliability, equity, academic integrity, and privacy. The educational potential of GenAI depends on pedagogical design and approaches that preserve learner autonomy and critical thinking. Further comparative studies assessing unassisted performance are needed to clarify its effects on learning.

items.title: Intelligent Scientific Literature Analysis with Generative AI: A Literature Review and Conceptual Framework
items.abstract: New research papers are published every day, and students and researchers cannot search, read, compare and summarize the relevant ones by hand without losing a lot of time. Generative AI tools, mainly large language models (LLMs), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), natural language processing (NLP) and AI agents, could cut some of that effort by finding papers, writing summaries, answering specific research questions and pulling out key findings. This paper looks at five works that run from Kitchenham's systematic review method to the LitLLM toolkit and compares their methods, findings and limitations. Six gaps came out of that comparison. Models sometimes invent things and cannot compare papers well. Large collections slow them down. Specialised fields are another weak spot, and they never show how they reached an answer. In the end a person has to check the result anyway. The paper then proposes an eight-stage conceptual framework that goes from database collection through NLP, retrieval, LLM reasoning and generative summarization to a final analysis report, along with evaluation measures and ethical points. The framework is only a concept; it has not been built or benchmarked.

items.title: Intraoperative artificial intelligence for brain tumor surgery: from tissue diagnosis to real-time surgical guidance
items.abstract: The 2021 WHO CNS tumor classification marked a fundamental shift in neuro-oncology: molecular markers rather than histological appearance now define glioma diagnosis and guide treatment. Yet, in clinical practice the molecular information that matters most to a surgeon—IDH status, 1p/19q codeletion, and methylation class—typically arrives days to weeks after the operation it was meant to inform. Artificial intelligence (AI) is beginning to close that gap. Over the past several years, a growing body of work has demonstrated that AI models can extract diagnostically relevant molecular and histological information from data sources available in the operating room, in real time, at the point of surgical decision-making. In this review, the authors provide a comprehensive overview of state-of-the-art intraoperative AI models available to neurosurgeons during brain tumor resections. They examine AI-augmented approaches to established intraoperative techniques, such as cryosection and fluorescence-guided surgery, before turning to novel technologies including nanopore sequencing and stimulated Raman histology (SRH). The authors conclude by discussing barriers to widespread clinical adoption and what lies ahead for this field. For cryosection, models such as LGNet and the Cryosection Histopathology Assessment and Review Machine (CHARM) have demonstrated strong performance on intraoperative discrimination of primary CNS lymphoma and molecular subtyping of glioma, respectively, with CHARM achieving areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.88–0.93 across glioma subtypes. In fluorescence-guided surgery, hyperspectral imaging combined with machine learning has enabled classification of tumor type, grade, and IDH mutation based on the 5-aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA) signal with up to 93% accuracy, extracting molecular information from a modality already present in the operating room. For nanopore-based methylation classification, ensemble models such as Rapid Nanopore Brain Intraoperative Classification (ROBIN) have achieved 90% concordance with the final diagnosis prospectively in under 2 hours. In SRH, foundation models for infiltration detection now outperform FLAIR, contrast enhancement, and 5-ALA fluorescence in identifying tumor margins, while molecular classification models have achieved over 90% glioma subtype accuracy in multi-institutional cohorts. At the single-cell level, morphometric profiling of SRH images has revealed nuclear features distinguishing IDH-mutant from IDH-wildtype tumors, opening new avenues for interpretability. Despite this progress, widespread adoption remains limited by the absence of randomized clinical trials demonstrating patient-level benefit. Addressing this gap and realizing the potential of multimodal AI systems that integrate imaging, pathology, and molecular data represent critical next steps for the field.

items.title: Introducing Artificial Intelligence into Surgical Practice for Cancer Care: Clinical Applications and Ethical Considerations
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in healthcare, but their utility in plastic surgery and skin cancer management remains in contention. Furthermore, the comparative performance of LLMs in the setting of skin cancer surgery is unclear. This study assessed four widely used LLMs and comparatively evaluated their relevance, accuracy, and clinical representativeness. Methods: This prospective study evaluated six standardised skin cancer prompts submitted to ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Copilot. Specialist plastic surgeons assessed textual responses for relevance and accuracy, and generated images for clinical representativeness and accuracy. Readability and DISCERN scores were also assessed. Results: All four LLMs produced highly relevant textual responses, with relevance scores ranging from 4 to 5, while accuracy scores ranged from 3 to 5. ChatGPT and Copilot achieved the highest individual accuracy scores. Only ChatGPT and Gemini generated images. ChatGPT demonstrated greater clinical representativeness and accuracy across all image prompts. ChatGPT produced the most linguistically complex responses, while Copilot produced the most readable outputs. All models generated text requiring at least a high-school level of education. Claude achieved the highest mean DISCERN score (43.67), followed by ChatGPT (40.33), Copilot (36.00), and Gemini (35.67). Conclusions: In this exploratory comparison, contemporary LLM-based platforms produced relevant and largely accurate skin cancer surgery information, but differed in image generation, readability, and information quality. The generated images depicted predominantly lighter skin tones, which warrants greater input from more diverse patient populations, and outputs should be used alongside clinician review. Larger studies using patient-specific scenarios and diverse skin tones are needed.

items.title: Introduction
items.abstract: This introduction sets the conceptual and contextual foundation for the edited volume by tracing the development of reflective practice (RP) in second language education (SLE) and examining its renewed significance in the digital era. It first situates RP within the work of Dewey and Schön and discusses its relevance for language teachers as thinking professionals who interpret complex classroom, institutional and sociocultural realities. The introduction then considers how digital technologies, including learning management systems, Eportfolios, video platforms, online communities, corpus tools, social media, chatbots, and generative AI, are reshaping the conditions under which teachers document, analyze and make sense of their professional experiences. While acknowledging the potential of these tools to extend and support reflection, it also highlights important concerns related to superficial engagement, performativity, surveillance, dependency and decontextualized feedback. The chapter outlines the main contributions of the volume, introduces its three-part organization, and argues for a human-centered, ethical, context-sensitive and professionally meaningful approach to technology-mediated RP in SLE.

items.title: Invasomes: A smart nanovesicular platform for enhanced transdermal drug delivery
items.abstract: Transdermal drug delivery systems (TDDS) provide a non-invasive alternative to oral and injectable administration; however, their clinical utility remains limited by the formidable barrier properties of the stratum corneum, which restrict the delivery of many therapeutic agents, particularly hydrophilic and high-molecular-weight molecules. Invasomes, composed of phospholipids, ethanol, and terpenes, have emerged as highly deformable nanovesicular carriers capable of enhancing skin permeation through synergistic lipid fluidization and vesicular flexibility. This review provides a comprehensive and updated overview of invasome-based transdermal drug delivery, distinguishing itself from previous reviews by integrating recent advances in formulation strategies, physicochemical characterization, penetration mechanisms, therapeutic applications, smart and hybrid invasomes, computational formulation design, regulatory considerations, and translational challenges. The review critically discusses the influence of formulation variables, including phospholipid composition, ethanol content, terpene type, and drug physicochemical properties, on vesicle characteristics, stability, encapsulation efficiency, and biological performance. Furthermore, recent in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo studies collectively demonstrate that invasomes significantly enhance skin permeation, drug deposition, bioavailability, and therapeutic efficacy compared with conventional vesicular systems while maintaining favorable safety profiles. Emerging innovations, including stimuli-responsive invasomes, microneedle-assisted delivery, artificial intelligence-guided formulation optimization, and molecular modeling, are also highlighted as promising approaches for next-generation transdermal therapies. Despite encouraging preclinical evidence, challenges related to large-scale manufacturing, long-term stability, regulatory standardization, and clinical validation remain to be addressed. Overall, this review provides a current and translational perspective on invasome technology and highlights its potential as a versatile nanovesicular platform for future clinical transdermal drug delivery.

items.title: Inverse design of lithium-ion battery microstructures using physics-constrained generative AI
items.abstract: The electrochemical performance of lithium-ion batteries is strongly governed by the complex three-dimensional architecture of porous electrodes. While recent advances in generative artificial intelligence have enabled realistic reconstruction of battery microstructures, existing approaches primarily focus on reproducing morphology or correlating manufacturing parameters with structural characteristics, providing limited control over transport-relevant properties. In this work, we develop a physics-constrained conditional generative adversarial network (PC-cGAN) for the inverse generation of LiNi 0.5 Mn 0.3 Co 0.2 O 2 , NMC532 cathode microstructures conditioned on target physical descriptors. The framework integrates a physical constraint network that enforces porosity, active-material volume fraction, and tortuosity during training, enabling direct generation of microstructures consistent with desired transport characteristics. Beyond morphology reconstruction, the framework also supports inverse microstructure design by mapping user-specified transport properties directly into three-dimensional, physically consistent electrode architectures. This functionality opens a pathway to probe structure-transport relationships that are otherwise challenging to isolate experimentally, while laying the groundwork for AI-enabled digital twins of battery electrodes. Coupling the framework with electrochemical and manufacturing simulations will enable virtual screening of architectures, accelerate optimization cycles, and advance physics-guided battery design with reduced experimental effort.

items.title: Invisible Gaze on Children: Addressing the Lacunas in EdTech Surveillance's Legal Framework in India
items.abstract: The digital revolution in India has touched every aspect of human endeavor from as basic as birth registration to Artificial Intelligence (“AI”) assisted scientific research. One of the most basic requirements- education is spurred by EdTech platforms. It offers students several opportunities and simultaneously exposes children to the risks of mass surveillance through data collection. The proliferation of virtual classrooms has enhanced the data collection, processing, and potential misuse of children's sensitive and personal information by the EdTech providers. This raises urgent questions about the legal protections and their adequacy within India's regulatory framework for protection of the children given the recent data commercialization and breaches in maintenance of children's data by Edtech. The aim of the study is to analyse the existing legal framework on the available protection and make recommendations that should feature in the rules that the government may make for the protection of children against the possible misuse by the EdTech companies. The study uses a doctrinal approach whereby the existing law will be analysed to unearth the loopholes in the context of child's right to privacy in EdTech offered classrooms. This analysis is fruitful for policy making in the area by mooting for an oversight mechanism to ensure compliance and fix liability in case of breach on the EdTech platforms.

items.title: Knowing When to Use Automation: Task-Specific Expertise and GPS Engagement in a Navigational Task
items.abstract: As automated systems become increasingly embedded in everyday consumer technologies, understanding how individual differences shape engagement decisions is critical for supporting users. The present study examined how task-specific expertise influences engagement with an optional GPS assistant across fourteen trials in a simulated map-based navigation task. Ninety-one undergraduate participants were classified as navigational experts or novices by accuracy on a task-specific knowledge test of the simulated maps. As hypothesized, experts engaged the GPS significantly less than novices. Despite the difference in engagement, navigational accuracy did not significantly differ between groups, suggesting that novices engaged the GPS at rates that compensated for their lower expertise bringing their performance to comparable levels of experts. Post-hoc analyses revealed that poorer spatial orientation was associated with greater GPS engagement and lower navigational expertise. These findings suggest individuals may make calibrated and capability driven decisions about their automation engagement.

items.title: Knowing Your Number Is Not Permission to Call: Authorization-to-Reach for Spam-Free, Privacy-First Communication in the 6G and AI-Agent Era
items.abstract: Abstract Robocalls, spam texts, and scam calls all exploit one design assumption: anyone who knows a phone number, SIP URI, or messaging handle can attempt contact. Once a number is shared with a business, a marketplace seller, a delivery driver, or a directory listing, it becomes a permanent, reusable route, and leaked or brokered contact data keeps that route open for anyone who obtains it. Existing defences answer different questions. STIR/SHAKEN verifies who is calling, not whether that caller is permitted to reach this recipient now. Virtual and masked numbers hide the real number but stay dialable while active. OAuth delegates API access but defines no telecom reachability rules. Spam scoring and call screening judge an attempt only after it has already been routed and signaled. This disclosure describes an authorization-to-reach model that separates knowing a contact identifier from permission to make contact. Each inbound call, message, or notification is held as a candidate request until an enforcement point, such as a session border controller, SIP application server, IMS node, or CPaaS gateway, validates a recipient-scoped grant bound to sender, recipient, purpose or transaction, channel, expiry, attempt quota, revocation epoch, and audience, with replay protection and sender binding so that a copied grant is not a bearer credential. Only then does the phone ring or the message get delivered; otherwise the request is rejected (for example with SIP 403) before any communication takes effect. Three deployment profiles, blocked path, pre-routing authorization, and absent path, allow incremental rollout over existing E.164 numbering, SIP, IMS, and PSTN infrastructure, while emergency calls (911/112) and lawful intercept remain unaffected. The gap grows as AI agents and AI-native 6G networks originate contact at machine speed. The record includes use cases (map and directory enquiries, marketplaces, ride and delivery, AI assistants), a comparison with existing approaches, a candidate grant format, possible STIR/PASSporT, SIP, and OAuth encodings, security and privacy analysis, a 58-question telecom engineering FAQ, and five workflow charts. A reference implementation is publicly available. Its central principle: possession of a communication identifier is not, by itself, permission to communicate. Download the full PDF to review the workflow charts, grant format, deployment profiles, and complete FAQ. items.title: Knowledge and meaning in a technology-driven world: a rapid review
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of digital technologies, such as Artificial Intelligence (AI), virtual and augmented reality, the Internet of Things (IoT), and the Internet of Everything (IoE), has reshaped human life, raising existential questions and challenging traditional sources of meaning. This study addresses the problem of how these technological transformations affect individuals’ processes of meaning-making and the management of knowledge in the digital era. The aim of this study is to examine the relationship between digital technologies, digital literacy, and knowledge management, with a particular focus on their implications for existential inquiry and meaningful engagement with technology. A rapid review methodology was applied to analyze 18 peer-reviewed studies indexed in Scopus, published between 2010 and 2024. The analysis explored their relevance to existentialism, meaning-making, and human existence in the context of digital technologies. The thematic analysis identified five key themes: AI and existential concerns, technology and human experience, embodied cognition and technology, digital literacy and knowledge management, and technology and meaningful interaction. The findings indicate that digital technologies substantially reshape identity, autonomy, and individuals’ search for meaning, while digital literacy emerges as a central capability for navigating these changes and supporting effective knowledge management. The study highlights important implications for research and practice, suggesting that strengthening digital literacy is essential to foster more meaningful interactions with technology and to mitigate potential negative existential and cognitive effects. Limitations include potential selection biases, reliance on self-reported data, and cultural and socioeconomic constraints that may affect the generalizability of the results.

items.abstract: This chapter examines knowledge graphs as the semantic integration backbone of next-generation research infrastructures. It traces the theoretical distinctions separating knowledge graphs from ontologies and relational schemas, surveys RDF-based storage and federated query architectures, and reviews ontology alignment, embedding-based representation learning, and knowledge graph completion as mechanisms for reconciling heterogeneous data sources. Applications across biomedicine, cultural heritage, bibliometrics, and recommendation are examined alongside the convergence of knowledge graphs with large language models for explainable, grounded reasoning. The chapter concludes by identifying scalability, governance, and provenance challenges facing research infrastructure architects designing federated, cognitively grounded data systems.

items.title: Knowledge Tracing and Student Modeling in Intelligent Tutoring Systems: A Systematic Literature Review of Computational Methods, Learner State Estimation, and Predictive Performance
items.abstract: Computer-based intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) use Student Modelling and Knowledge Tracing (KT) at the core of adaptive learning environments to model and predict each learner's mastery. While conversational AI improves pedagogical feedback, the core adaptability of ITS ultimately depends on strong Educational Data Mining (EDM) and Learning Analytics (LA) algorithms. Existing literature reviews often conflate frontend instructional AI with backend analytics, leaving a critical gap in synthesizing the computational approaches and predictive systems that drive these intelligent systems. To address this gap, a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted following PRISMA guidelines, systematically analysing 15 high-quality studies focused only on the computational dimensions of ITS. The results show a clear model shift away from simple traditional probabilistic models towards the latest versions of deep-learning based classic DKT architectures, including context-aware gating and Transformer networks. Learner state representations are also increasingly complex and add behavioural interaction histories rather than simple testing observations of correct or incorrect outcomes. While the validity of these data-driven models continues to be high (particularly in well-structured domains like mathematics), their real-world operational challenges are much harder to resolve, with major technical issues of data sparsity, algorithmic bias, sustainability of pedagogic fit and the diffuse "black-box" of deep neural networks common across the literature. These issues mean that future researches, defined by the authors as the ongoing interaction between the computational and human, should seek to develop explainable AI (XAI) and fairness-aware algorithms that support scalable, trusted human-AI teaming.

items.title: KnowTI: Bridging the Knowledge Gap in Information Communication through Interactive Visual LLM Summarizations
items.abstract: Abstract The gap between expert knowledge and layperson understanding often poses challenges to the effective communication of unfamiliar concepts. To address this issue, we introduce a semi‐automated, interactive visual summarization framework with modularity and user control, KnowTI, which leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) and visualization methods to facilitate knowledge transfer. Our approach aims to narrow the knowledge gap of laypersons in comprehending complex information as presented by experts, while remaining engaged, making our solution applicable to a variety of information communication contexts—including, but not limited to, educational videos. We validate the effectiveness of KnowTI through a comparative study with 40 participants, contrasting our approach with traditional video‐based learning. Findings indicate that KnowTI not only enhances knowledge acquisition and engagement, but also supports laypersons in understanding complex, domain‐specific topics, bridging the knowledge gap between experts and non‐experts. items.title: Large language model-assisted modern programming pedagogy model: a perspective on teaching programming in the era of LLMs
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are a double-edged technology. They can serve as learning assistants in programming while simultaneously raising pedagogical and ethical concerns. Programming education researchers have responded by providing guidelines and recommendations on teaching, assessment, and the ethical use of LLMs. Although these developments are welcome, the literature still lacks theory-based frameworks that provide a philosophical grounding for programming pedagogy. This perspective paper addresses this gap by proposing the LLM-Assisted Modern Programming Pedagogy (LAMPP) model. The model aims to provide a theory-informed framework for systematically guiding the integration of LLMs into programming pedagogy. It proposes four design principles encompassing the core components of pedagogy (i.e., teaching, lesson design, engagement, and assessment). Ethics is included as an additional dimension because ethical concerns cut across all aspects of pedagogy. The LAMPP model proposes different mechanisms that may mitigate potential learning losses associated with inappropriate or excessive reliance on LLMs. Future studies should test the effectiveness of these mechanisms. The model may provide a basis for educators, researchers, and policymakers when considering policies, curriculum structures, course outcomes, assessment practices, and ethical guidelines related to programming pedagogy. In summary, it is not about LLM tools themselves but about the pedagogical orchestration of these technologies in programming education.

items.title: Large Language Model-Assisted Multimodal Federated Sensing for Compliance Risk Screening in Cross-Border Trade
items.abstract: With the continuous expansion of cross-border agricultural supply chains, reliable food-safety risk screening under decentralized data ownership, heterogeneous sensing equipment, and jurisdiction-dependent, non-stationary regulatory limits pose a fundamental challenge to intelligent inspection systems. To address these limitations, this paper proposes an LLM-assisted regulation-aware heterogeneous multimodal federated learning framework that establishes a three-tier decoupling architecture. First, an available-modality and quality-adaptive fusion mechanism dynamically weights RGB images, near-infrared (NIR) spectra, and environmental time-series while enforcing strict zero weighting on unavailable modalities and continuous suppression of degraded observations. Second, a regulation-independent state-prototype collaboration and personalized federated learning strategy is developed on a unified continuous concentration scale, enabling cross-institutional transfer of physical contamination representations while avoiding the use of jurisdiction-dependent compliance labels to define shared prototype groups and preserving client-specific adapters against non-IID drift. Third, offline large language model (LLM) parsing transforms unstructured multi-jurisdictional trade regulations into machine-executable rule bases, which are coupled with an uncertainty-aware risk calibration module to dynamically determine exceedance probabilities and reinspection recommendations without retraining front-end sensing encoders when regulatory standards shift. Experimental evaluations on a multisource maize and aflatoxin B1 screening dataset in a workstation-based federated simulation demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.054±0.002 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.078±0.003, while elevating the area under the curve (AUC) and F1-score to 0.862±0.008 and 0.833±0.009, respectively, reducing the false negative rate (FNR) to 0.121±0.007 (p<0.001). Under severe client heterogeneity and missing-modality scenarios, the proposed approach maintains an AUC of 0.823±0.010 and an F1-score of 0.796±0.011. Ablation and ownership-level analyses assess robustness, calibration (expected calibration error of 0.032), and regulatory adaptation with fixed sensing encoders, providing an end-to-end, traceable decision-support paradigm for international agricultural trade screening.

items.title: Large Language Model-Assisted Title and Abstract Screening for A Scoping Review of Circulating miRNA Monitoring: Pilot Validation Against a Human Reviewer and Quantifying the Error of Keyword Pre-Filters
items.abstract: This study evaluated an open-weight LLM and keyword rules for title/abstract screening of circulating microRNA (miRNA) monitoring biomarker reviews. PubMed and Europe PMC searches returned 3,204 records (1,976 after deduplication). Automated keyword rules excluded 1,222 records; 754 were screened by gpt-oss-120b (n = 628) or gpt-oss-20b (n = 126) at temperature 0. One reviewer labelled 225 records; a second independently labelled a stratified 113-record sample, and 21 disagreements were adjudicated to consensus (2 Include, 3 Maybe, 16 Exclude), serving as the reference, though blinding of the first reviewer to LLM outputs could not be verified. The primary outcome was sensitivity for Include or Maybe against a pre-set threshold of 0.95. The LLM returned Include 173, Maybe 102, and Exclude 479. Against the consensus reference, sensitivity was 0.89 (95% CI 0.77–0.95), specificity 0.90 (95% CI 0.83–0.95), and kappa 0.65 (95% CI 0.54–0.76). Of 100 randomly sampled LLM-excluded records, 5 (5%) were reference-Include; in all five, the LLM's stated reason involved prognostic or clinical-event outcomes rather than drug response, resistance, or toxicity. Among keyword-excluded records, 11/75 (15%) were reference-Include, rising to 11/50 (22%) for the rule 'no human circulating miRNA + treatment context'. The sensitivity point estimate fell below 0.95, but its 95% CI (0.77–0.95) includes 0.95, so this pilot cannot rule out that the threshold is met; keyword pre-filters excluded relevant records at a rate that made them unsafe without audit. In this domain, an LLM can prioritise records but cannot replace human screening. The authors propose clearer outcome criteria, single-model runs, stratified human audits of every automated exclusion, and pre-registered performance thresholds.

items.title: Large Language Model–Driven Frameworks for Intelligent Cyberbullying Detection and Prevention
items.abstract: This chapter analyzes published work on the use of large language models (LLMs) in smart frameworks for the detection and prevention of cyberbullying across social media, gaming, and learning platforms. The data shows a clear movement from the use of traditional machine learning and earlier deep learning models to the application of LLMs that possess capabilities of understanding and processing context, which allow them to identify and categorize abuses of the online environment that are subtle and implicit, as well as those that use multiple modalities and languages. The literature shows the following recurring themes: use of prompt-engineered LLMs for cyberbullying detection with little or no training; hybrid models that integrate LLMs with classical machine learning; moderation models; and conversational agents for real-time, empathetic abuse interventions. Other themes include increased focus on bias and fairness, explainability, data scarcity, and domain adaptation for high-risk systems and safety. The chapter provides this structure by first assessing foundational literature on automated detection of cyberbullying and toxic language, then LLM-based detection architectures and LLM-enabled prevention and intervention strategies, such as counseling chatbots and bystander aid tools. The subsequent sections integrate the literature on evaluation methodologies, benchmark datasets, and the spatial and temporal adversity and abusive behavior countermeasure robustness, then address the specific ethical, legal, and policy LLM online safety ecosystem deployment issues. This extensive literature review provides a synthesis of the LLM literature on online safety tools, determines converging design strategies and unresolved issues, and articulates design principles for LLM-based tools that promote safer online communities.

items.title: Large language models for complex decision-making in colorectal cancer with peritoneal metastases
items.abstract: Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated for oncology decision support, but their performance in colorectal cancer with peritoneal metastases (CRC-PM) remains uncertain. We benchmarked 10 contemporary LLMs against an expert-consensus framework. Methods Forty-eight synthetic vignettes were derived from a 2026 CRC-PM consensus guideline, including 36 primary scenarios and 12 counterfactual scenarios forming six pairs. Each model completed every vignette three times using a frozen zero-shot structured prompt. The primary endpoint was prompt-aligned structured Full concordance; contradiction-only and full-semantic adjudication were sensitivity analyses. Two blinded attending colorectal surgeons, each with 5 years of clinical experience, independently validated the reference classifications. Results Among 1,080 primary responses, structured scoring classified 609 (56.4%) as Full, 117 (10.8%) as Partial, and 354 (32.8%) as Discordant. Model-specific structured Full concordance ranged from 49.1% to 63.0%; neither the Friedman test ( P = .104) nor clustered GEE ( P = .186) supported a robust model effect. Contradiction-only scoring was similar (56.2% Full), whereas full-semantic adjudication reduced Full concordance to 45.5%. Excluding prompt-development scenarios lowered absolute concordance but did not change the inferential conclusion. Expert agreement was 93.8%–97.9% across decision domains (Cohen kappa 0.898–0.948). Counterfactual and metachronous risk-management analyses showed wide uncertainty, and 21 clinically consequential discordance flags arose from five scenarios. Conclusions LLM performance in CRC-PM was sensitive to scoring definition and did not establish a stable between-model hierarchy. Prospective clinician-plus-LLM studies are required before clinical benefit can be inferred.

items.abstract: Through architecture, aesthetics, and material agency, ecological consciousness unfolds as a journey across scales. Thus, this book’s conclusion proposes a final time–space transscalar journey from the Paleolithic cave in France to current lunar and deep-sea explorations aimed at expanding the human condition through artificial intelligence. The ultimate demonstration underscores the urgent need to cherish and reclaim the chirotopian spaces threatened by excessive material abstraction. Therefore, the ordinary spaces within reach, fostered within architectural spaces, can not only propel the construction of a new cosmology that recognizes vibrant matter but also amplify the distinct sensibility that makes us human.

items.title: LEAF: benchmarking multiobjective evolutionary feature selection over large language model–extracted symptoms for interpretable Traditional Chinese Medicine respiratory syndrome differentiation
items.abstract: Differentiating Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) respiratory syndromes requires weighing overlapping symptoms together with tongue and pulse findings, a task that most AI systems for TCM perform end-to-end but without an interpretable intermediate representation. In this study, we addressed this gap with LEAF (LLM extraction and multiobjective feature selection), a two-stage modular framework evaluated on 3,253 records covering 14 respiratory syndromes from the TCM-SD benchmark. Its first large language model (LLM) stage extracted a 35-item symptom ontology that was built entirely from public TCM sources; among three interchangeable LLMs, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct was ranked as the best, followed by Phi-4 and the TCM domain model BianCang. Its second evolutionary-computation stage benchmarked four multiobjective evolutionary algorithms [non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm-II (NSGA-II), strength Pareto evolutionary algorithm 2 (SPEA2), competitive mechanism-based multiobjective particle swarm optimizer (CMOPSO), and non-dominated sorting differential evolution (NSDE)] over 10 seeds, and they were compared using Friedman’s and Nemenyi’s testing in terms of both classification outcome and search-process quality. The four algorithms showed no significant separation on held-out macro-F1, although NSDE led nominally, and none exceeded the full-feature baseline on point estimates. In contrast, hypervolume differed significantly and favored NSGA-II, the weakest of the four on held-out macro-F1. A four-classifier panel found no algorithm to be significantly different from either the full-feature baseline or a random-feature control, which was significantly outperformed only by the full-feature baseline. Applying NSDE to the remaining two LLM pipelines reproduced the original ranking, and its representative solution was fully attested against the knowledge base of TCM-SD, although not typically so across all the 10 seeds. These results show that an LLM-extraction frontend built exclusively from public knowledge can provide a representation over which evolutionary feature selection cuts the candidate feature set roughly in half without a statistically detectable cost in performance, albeit at a small point-estimate cost; that hypervolume and inverted generational distance are not reliable stand-ins for classification-relevant algorithm selection here; and that a no-gold-standard proxy evaluation can substitute human annotation when expert time is limited. Because both stages plug in and out freely, the framework can absorb stronger components in either stage as they become available.

items.title: Learning engagement and creative self-beliefs in generative AI-supported design education: self-reported prompt literacy and dimensions of AI dependence
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is changing how design students learn, yet little is known about how students’ perceived capability to work with GenAI relates to their learning engagement and motivational self-beliefs, or under which forms of AI dependence this link is weaker. Drawing on social cognitive theory, this cross-sectional study examined self-reported prompt literacy, learning engagement, and two components of the creative self: creative self-efficacy (CSE), a motivational belief in one’s creative capability, and creative personal identity (CPI), the importance of creativity to one’s self-concept. Survey data came from 829 undergraduate art and design students in 40 intact classes at two institutions in mainland China; latent-variable and moderation models accounted for the clustering of students within classes. Self-reported prompt literacy was positively associated with engagement ( β = 0.54), and engagement was positively associated with both CSE ( β = 0.62) and CPI ( β = 0.47). Engagement was more strongly associated with CSE than with CPI (difference = 0.14, 95% CI [0.04, 0.24]) and remained uniquely associated with CPI after CSE was taken into account. When four dimensions of AI dependence were modeled simultaneously, the prompt literacy–engagement association was weaker among students reporting higher cognitive dependence; evidence for loss of control was weaker, and functional and emotional dependence showed no clear unique moderation. All interaction effects were small. The dimensional analysis identified cognitive dependence as the clearest moderator. These cross-sectional, self-reported findings suggest possible boundary conditions for the capability–engagement association and require longitudinal and behavioral testing.

items.title: Learning under privileged information: a survey
items.abstract: Real-world learning scenarios often exhibit asymmetries between training and inference, where additional or higher-quality information is available only during training. The Learning Under Privileged Information (LUPI) paradigm provides a formal framework to study such settings. Despite research interest over the years, the extensive literature on LUPI remains highly fragmented. In this survey, we present a comprehensive and structured overview of research on LUPI and its related formulations. We review 107 papers published between 2009 and 2025 and propose a novel unified taxonomy based on two core dimensions: the underlying machine learning models, spanning both shallow and deep architectures, and the methodological strategies used to integrate privileged information. Additionally, we provide an extensive overview of the various application domains and the particular types of privileged modalities used. We also discuss key insights and open challenges, focusing on how and when privileged information can be effectively leveraged in modern machine learning systems.

items.title: Literature Review of Software Architectures for Developing Artificial Intelligence-Based Mobile Adaptive Learning Systems
items.abstract: The widespread adoption of mobile devices has driven the development of diverse educational technologies. In this context, Artificial Intelligence-based Mobile Adaptive Learning Systems (AI-based MALS) have emerged as an efficient alternative to complement the teaching and learning process. However, the advancement of these systems is hindered by significant challenges such as insufficient software architectural support, lack of standardization, and inadequate requirements coverage and correctness. Addressing these challenges requires designing high-quality software architectures. Accordingly, research focused on the design, development, and evaluation of software architectures for AI-based MALS is critical from a software engineering standpoint. Although some secondary studies have explored related topics through literature reviews and systematic mapping, no comprehensive secondary review has identified the principal architectural aspects of AI-based MALS design. This study conducts a Literature Review (LR) of software architectures that integrate Artificial Intelligence into Mobile Adaptive Learning Systems. The main objective is to identify and compare the critical aspects of software architectures for proposed AI-based MALS in the specialized literature. The findings highlight several essential elements that software architectures for AI-based MALS should address, including requirements, quality attributes, stakeholders, user services, architectural views and styles, components, and implementation technologies. The primary finding of this study is the absence of a reference software architecture in the reviewed studies that comprehensively addresses the requirements needed to develop AI-based MALS to support adaptive learning in mobile distributed environments.

items.title: LLM-DNN Fusion for Data-Efficient Trajectory Generation in Autonomous Driving: A Hybrid Approach with MPC Optimization
items.abstract: Autonomous vehicle (AV) trajectory planning in dense urban environments requires models that generalize to rare or previously unseen scenario types. Deep neural networks (DNNs) trained on large datasets perform poorly in such data-scarce conditions, while large language models (LLMs) generalize well but lack the numerical precision required for low-level vehicle control. This paper presents a hybrid trajectory planning framework that fuses a finetuned LLM with a multi-branch DNN at the trajectory level and applies a Model Predictive Control (MPC) controller as a final optimization stage. Gemini 1.5 Flash, fine-tuned on 479 labeled scenario-trajectory pairs, generates 15- aypoint trajectory proposals from structured textual scene descriptions. A modular DNN processes the same scene as a numerical input vector and produces a parallel trajectory proposal. The two proposals are fused by a learned trajectory refinement network, and the output is passed to an MPC controller that enforces vehicle dynamics constraints while minimizing a multi-objective cost function. Training relies on a three-step distortion- based augmentation technique, curve distortion, scale distortion, and Gaussian smoothing, that generates semi-realistic trajectory variants from a base dataset of over 70,000 labeled rows, reducing the data volume required for effective DNN training. Evaluation across 200 runs in the CARLA simulator on unseen urban scenarios shows that the MPC-enhanced hybrid model achieves an Average Displacement Error (ADE) of 0.66 m and a Final Displacement Error (FDE) of 1.94 m, corresponding to improvements of 37.7% and 34.3% over the DNN-only baseline. The collision rate (CR) decreases from 3.71% to 2.90%, a 21.8% reduction. These results establish that trajectory-level fusion of LLM semantic reasoning with DNN-based feature extraction delivers measurable accuracy and safety gains in data-efficient autonomous driving conditions. The ADE/FDE improvements are statistically significant (p < 0.001). The collision-rate reduction is a consistent trend across ablations, but it is not statistically significant at n = 200 runs (see Section 4.4).

items.title: LLM‐Enhanced Semantic Information Alignment for ID Recommendation
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Identity‐based Recommendation (IDR) plays a crucial role in modern personalized recommendation systems by leveraging users' identity information and historical interactions to model long‐term user preferences. However, existing IDR methods face three critical challenges: difficulty in fully capturing latent user preference, limited representational capacity, and poor adaptability to cold‐start scenarios. To address these issues, we propose the LLM‐Enhanced Semantic Information Alignment for ID Recommendation (ESIA‐IDR) framework, which systematically integrates semantic features generated by large language models (LLMs) into ID‐based recommendation. ESIA‐IDR first employs LLMs to deeply perceive unstructured textual data, such as user reviews and product descriptions, thereby effectively mining users' latent interest patterns. An independent pretraining mechanism is then applied to optimize the training dynamics of semantic and ID embeddings, mitigating inconsistencies in convergence behavior. Additionally, a feature discretization strategy is adopted to enhance semantic feature compatibility with traditional recommendation pipelines. During the recommendation phase, semantic‐enhanced features and collaborative signals are jointly modeled to achieve robust performance in cold‐start environments. ESIA‐IDR consists of four key components: Semantic and Interest Perception, Semantic Alignment, Discrete Feature Construction, and Recommendation Integration. By combining pretraining, dimensionality reduction, and similarity‐based bucketing, the framework achieves effective alignment between semantic features and ID feature spaces, bridging the semantic‐structural gap and improving user preference modeling accuracy. Extensive experiments on multiple real‐world datasets demonstrate that ESIA‐IDR achieves a 2.21% improvement in NDCG and a 1.48% improvement in Hit Rate compared to the best‐performing baselines, validating its effectiveness in enhancing recommendation performance.

items.title: LLMs for Transforming Data-Driven Research Discovery
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are rapidly reshaping the landscape of data-driven research discovery, offering unprecedented capabilities in natural language understanding, knowledge synthesis, and intelligent query resolution. This chapter explores the transformative role of LLMs within next-generation research infrastructures, examining how these models augment traditional data pipelines, accelerate hypothesis generation, and enable cross-domain knowledge integration. A proposed methodology integrating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), domain-adaptive fine-tuning, and semantic indexing is presented and evaluated on multi-disciplinary research corpora. Experimental results demonstrate significant gains in retrieval accuracy, citation relevance, and researcher productivity. The chapter further discusses practical advantages, persistent challenges including hallucination and bias, and a forward-looking perspective on human-AI collaborative research ecosystems.
